name: Jamaican Patois

ancestors.notes: English (via British English, Hiberno-English and Scots dialects of 17th-century slaveholders and overseers) is the lexifier of Jamaican Patois.

Akan (Twi) substrate, the largest single African contributor: se 'that' < Ashanti Twi, duppy 'ghost' < Twi dupon, obeah < Ashanti Twi Ɔbayi (Cassidy & Le Page 1980; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_Patois).
Igbo substrate: unu 'you (pl.)' < Igbo (Cassidy & Le Page 1980; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_Patois).
Yoruba substrate: de 'to be (at a location)' < Yoruba (Cassidy & Le Page 1980; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaican_Patois).

notes: Jamaican Patois (Jumiekan Kryuol) written in the Cassidy/JLU orthography (Cassidy 1961; standardised by the Jamaican Language Unit, UWI Mona, 2002). Phonemic by design: short vowels i e a o u; long vowels doubled (ii, aa, uu); diphthongs <ie> <uo> <ai> <ou>; <ch>=/tʃ/, <j>=/dʒ/, <sh>=/ʃ/, <zh>=/ʒ/, <ng>=/ŋ/. Nasal vowels are written with a following -hn (e.g. kyaahn); that convention is not modelled here. <ky> and <gy> are read as the single palatalised velars [kʲ] [ɡʲ]: Harry 2006 derives [ɡʲaːd] 'guard' and [kʲuː] by palatalisation of a velar obstruent before a front-vowel + back-vowel sequence, and his 21-consonant inventory has no palatal stop. The palatal stops /c/ /ɟ/ of Cassidy & Le Page 1967/1980 are the older phonemic analysis of the same onsets and are superseded by that account. /h/ is variable across Jamaica. Note: much Patois is also written in ad-hoc English-based spelling, which this spec does NOT cover — Cassidy/JLU input is assumed.
